The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari. Robert Wiene's 1920 German Expressionist psychological thriller in which a mysterious carnival hypnotist and his somnambulist assistant commit a series of murders in a twisted town. Distorted sets, harsh shadows, and an unreliable narrator create a nightmare aesthetic that became the visual DNA of German Expressionism and defined psychological horror cinema.

The film's world is visually distorted. Buildings lurch at impossible angles. Shadows are painted onto the sets. Perspective warps. The architecture embodies psychological fracture. Expressionist painters Hermann Warm, Walter Röhrig, and Walter Reimann designed these sets, making this a collaboration between fine art and cinema.

Dr. Caligari, a hypnotist, awakens the somnambulist Cesare each night to commit murders. The protagonist Francis investigates while falling into paranoia and conspiracy. The famous twist ending reveals the narrator may be unreliable or insane, raising questions about whether Caligari himself is the villain or a manifestation of the narrator's fractured mind. Production design became psychological expression: distorted geometry, chiaroscuro lighting, and painted shadows all reinforce the film's mood of creeping dread.

The Cabinet influenced Expressionist cinema across Europe and inspired the aesthetic vocabulary of film noir, German New Cinema, and psychological thrillers for a century. The film was nearly lost but survives in complete restoration, demonstrating how fragile these silent prints could be and how valuable preservation has become. It established the vocabulary of paranoia and unreliable narration in film, founded a tradition of psychological over visceral fear, and stands alongside fellow Expressionist masterpieces sharing shadow and distortion as the grammar of horror.
